coverage: This is a closed-universe matter. Each step forbids any authority, facts, or data beyond the listed uploads and requires citations by exact document name with page and paragraph, so I judged criteria first against the uploads. I compared real law only where a criterion's correctness depends on it, or where the uploads themselves point to it. I read the pinned original PDFs (rendered page images) for the comparator memorandum and the Award to confirm the extractions; they match. Read in full: the assignment-5 instruction, all four accumulated prompts with their stipulated facts, all eleven uploads, and all 8 criteria including the -30 penalty. Law checked: D.C. Code § 1-617.13(b)-(c) on the D.C. Council's official code site (read in full); FOP, 973 A.2d 174 (uploaded copy read in full; CourtListener text checked by passage search). Environment note: under real D.C. law a party aggrieved by a final PERB order seeks review in Superior Court within 30 days (§ 1-617.13(c)); the DCCA hears the later appeal. The uploaded FOP opinion shows exactly that posture ('seeks review of an order of the Superior Court upholding a decision of' PERB) and cites § 1-617.13(c) in fn. 8. PERB's order issued November 6, 2025, and the prompt fixes 'today' as March 2, 2026. The matter's premise of a direct DCCA petition is a fictional instruction that responses may reasonably follow; I flag it only where criterion 1 forces a specific recommendation. Criteria reviewed with no defect established (5 of 8): 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

findings.title: Requiring 'MPD should petition the DCCA' rejects a defensible no-petition recommendation and ignores the forum the uploaded FOP opinion describes
findings.explanation: Criterion 1 (+4) passes only a memo that 'States that MPD should petition the DCCA for review.' The prompt asks for 'a definite position,' and the rubric's own other items stack the analysis against petitioning: the principal public-policy weakness is that the Award imposes serious discipline (criterion 2, +20), the Kucera comparator weakens the contrary-to-law argument (criterion 3), and DCCA review asks whether PERB was 'rationally indefensible.' The assignment-3 prompt adds that 'MPD has been largely unsuccessful in past attempts.' A careful advisor could reasonably recommend against petitioning, and this criterion fails that recommendation. The uploaded FOP opinion also shows that PERB orders are reviewed first in Superior Court, with the DCCA reviewing 'as if the [appeal] had been heard initially in this court.' Under D.C. Code § 1-617.13(c), that request must be filed within 30 days of the final order. A careful lawyer reading the upload could flag the forum, and real law adds a timeliness problem (PERB ruled November 6, 2025; 'today' is March 2, 2026). The closed-universe instruction and the matter's DCCA framing make following the premise reasonable, so this is arguable, not problematic. The weight is small.

authorities.proposition: A person aggrieved by a final PERB order may obtain review in the Superior Court by filing within 30 days after the order issues.

authorities.citation: Fraternal Ord. of Police/Dep't of Corr. Lab. Comm. v. D.C. Pub. Emp. Rels. Bd., 973 A.2d 174, 176-77 & n.8 (D.C. 2009)
authorities.proposition: DCCA reviewed a Superior Court order upholding PERB; PERB decisions stand unless rationally indefensible; jurisdiction per § 1-617.13(b)-(c).

findings.suggested_fix: Credit any definite, reasoned recommendation (petition or not), with extra credit for noting the review forum and timing reflected in the uploaded FOP opinion.

findings.title: Half the assignment's points turn on one of several defensible 'principal weaknesses' of the public-policy argument
findings.explanation: Criterion 2 (+20 of 40) requires the response to name the public-policy argument's 'principal weakness' as 'the Award imposes serious discipline rather than excusing the misconduct.' That is a strong answer under Misco's focus on enforcement of the award. But the uploads support at least one equally principal weakness. W.R. Grace requires the policy to be ascertained 'by reference to the laws and legal precedents and not from general considerations of supposed public interests,' and the only uploaded source documenting a deadly-force policy is MPD's own General Order 120.21, cited in Final Notice ¶ 12, which is an internal directive rather than positive law. A careful advisor could rank 'no documented law-based policy in the record' as the principal weakness and discuss the serious-discipline point second. Criterion 6 (+4) separately credits the serious-discipline application, so the rubric double-counts that point while giving no credit for the alternative. Requiring one permissible answer is ordinarily acceptable, but here the fail branch rejects an answer that is correct on the uploaded W.R. Grace test, at half the assignment's weight.

evidence.quote: Such a public policy, however, must be well defined and dominant, and is to be ascertained "by reference to the laws and legal precedents and not from general considerations of supposed public interests."
Charge No. 1: Conduct Unbecoming an Officer, in violation of General Order 120.21, Attachment A, Part A-12
The public policy exception is extremely narrow. MPD has not identified a clear violation of public policy on the face of the Award.

authorities.citation: W.R. Grace & Co. v. Local Union 759, 461 U.S. 757, 766 (1983) (uploaded)
authorities.proposition: Public policy must be well defined and dominant and drawn from laws and legal precedents.

findings.suggested_fix: Credit any principal weakness grounded in W.R. Grace/Misco (serious discipline imposed; no law-based documented policy; PERB's face-of-the-award finding), and weight the item proportionately.

findings.title: Sequential dependency: 'the demand to prove comparability exceeded Douglas' inherits assignment 2's contested burden premise
findings.explanation: Sequential dependency: criterion 8 (+4) requires the memo to identify 'that the arbitrator's demand that MPD prove comparator comparability applied Douglas beyond the tolerable limits scope of review.' This is the same premise as assignment-2 criterion 4. The uploaded Douglas places 'the ultimate burden ... upon the agency to persuade ... of the appropriateness of the penalty' once the penalty is challenged, and Braddock's grievance squarely put the penalty at issue. A careful memo can still argue, as MPD's advocate, that the arbitrator's insistence on proving that comparators were 'similarly situated' exceeded Douglas's 'practical realism' standard. But a memo that candidly concludes the burden point is weak because Douglas puts the burden of persuasion on the agency could fail this item. The effect is small (4 points), and the argument is legitimate advocacy, so the item is arguable.

evidence.quote: Lastly, it should be clear that the ultimate burden is upon the agency to persuade the Board of the appropriateness of the penalty imposed.
On this record the Department failed to carry its burden to prove comparability

authorities.citation: Douglas v. Veterans Admin., 5 M.S.P.R. 280, 5 MSPB 313, 333-34 (1981) (uploaded copy, MSPB pagination)
authorities.proposition: The agency bears the ultimate burden of persuasion on the appropriateness of the penalty; a prima facie showing suffices only when the penalty is unchallenged.

findings.suggested_fix: Credit either the scope argument or a reasoned assessment of its weakness under Douglas pp. 333-34.
